knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)

## Introduction

Real projects start with a file that someone else collected. In this lab, you import a CSV file of student grades and apply conditional statements to it. Then you export the cleaned results. Each part ends with a question, and each answer comes from the output you see when you run the code.

## Part A: Examples of Conditional Statements

A conditional statement lets R choose what to do based on a `TRUE` or `FALSE` condition.

### Example A: if ... else

```{r exA}
score <- 78

if (score >= 75) {
  print("Passed")
} else {
  print("Failed")
}
```

The score of 78 meets the cutoff of 75, so R prints "Passed". A score of 74 prints "Failed".

### Example B: if ... else if ... else

```{r exB}
score <- 86

if (score >= 90) {
  print("Excellent")
} else if (score >= 80) {
  print("Good")
} else if (score >= 75) {
  print("Fair")
} else {
  print("Needs Improvement")
}
```

R checks the tests from top to bottom and stops at the first `TRUE`. The score of 86 fails the first test and passes the second, so R prints "Good". It never reaches the "Fair" test.

### Example C: ifelse() on a vector

```{r exC}
scores <- c(92, 68, 75, 81, 59)
ifelse(scores >= 75, "Passed", "Failed")
```

The function tests all five scores at once. Scores of 92, 75, and 81 pass. Scores of 68 and 59 fail.

### Example D: combining conditions

```{r exD}
grade <- 91
attendance <- 95

if (grade >= 90 & attendance >= 90) {
  print("Honors candidate")
}
```

Both conditions are `TRUE`, so R prints the message. Use `&` when both conditions must hold. Use `|` when one is enough. An attendance of 85 prints nothing, since this `if` has no `else` branch.

## Part B: Conditional Statements

### Question #1

```{r q1}
temp <- 33

if (temp >= 32) {
  print("Hot")
} else {
  print("Not hot")
}
```

The temperature of 33 is above 32, so R prints "Hot".

### Question #2

```{r q2}
age <- 17

if (age < 13) {
  print("Child")
} else if (age <= 19) {
  print("Teenager")
} else {
  print("Adult")
}
```

The age of 17 fails the first test and passes the second, so R prints "Teenager".

### Question #3

```{r q3}
marks <- c(45, 88, 73, 100, 62)
result <- ifelse(marks >= 60, "Pass", "Fail")
print(result)
```

Only the mark of 45 falls below 60. The other four marks pass.

### Question #4

```{r q4}
x <- 10

if (x > 5) {
  print("A")
} else if (x > 8) {
  print("B")
} else {
  print("C")
}

# Prediction: R prints "A".
# The test x > 5 is TRUE for 10, so R runs that block and skips the rest.
# The test x > 8 is also TRUE for 10, but R never checks it.
```

### Question #5

The `if` statement tests one value and runs one block of code. The `ifelse()` function tests every element of a vector and returns a vector of the same length. I choose `if` to control the flow of a script with a single condition. I choose `ifelse()` to build a new column from a whole column of data.

## Part C: Importing the CSV File

### Question #6

Import the file safely. The `stop()` call halts the knit at once with a clear message, so a missing file never causes a confusing error later.

```{r import}
file_name <- "students_grades.csv"

if (file.exists(file_name)) {
  grades <- read.csv(file_name, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  print("File imported.")
} else {
  stop("File not found. Save students_grades.csv in the same folder as this .Rmd file.")
}
```

Inspect the data.

```{r inspect}
head(grades)
dim(grades)
str(grades)
summary(grades)
colSums(is.na(grades))
```

Answer the questions.

```{r answers}
nrow(grades)
ncol(grades)
names(which(colSums(is.na(grades)) > 0))
class(grades$Section)
range(grades$Attendance)
```

- The data frame has 15 rows and 7 columns.
- The Midterm column holds the one missing value. It belongs to Bea Navarro.
- The Section column has the character type.
- The lowest Attendance is 70 and the highest is 100.

Check the structure.

```{r check1}
stopifnot(nrow(grades) == 15, ncol(grades) == 7, sum(is.na(grades)) == 1)
print("Check passed: 15 rows, 7 columns, 1 NA.")
```

### Applying Conditional Statements

**f.1 Final grade.** Any arithmetic with `NA` gives `NA`. Bea Navarro has no midterm score, so her final grade is `NA`. This is expected.

```{r f1}
grades$FinalGrade <- 0.30 * grades$Quiz + 0.30 * grades$Midterm + 0.40 * grades$Final
grades[, c("Name", "FinalGrade")]
```

**f.2 Pass or fail.** The `NA` check comes first. The comparison `NA >= 75` returns `NA`, not `TRUE` or `FALSE`.

```{r f2}
grades$Result <- ifelse(is.na(grades$FinalGrade), "Incomplete",
                 ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 75, "Passed", "Failed"))
table(grades$Result)
```

**f.3 Grade remarks.**

```{r f3}
grades$Remarks <- ifelse(is.na(grades$FinalGrade), "Incomplete",
                  ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 90, "Excellent",
                  ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 85, "Very Good",
                  ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 80, "Good",
                  ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 75, "Fair", "Needs Improvement")))))
table(grades$Remarks)
```

**f.4 Attendance flag.**

```{r f4}
grades$AttendanceFlag <- ifelse(grades$Attendance < 80, "At Risk", "OK")
table(grades$AttendanceFlag)
```

**f.5 Honors candidates.** The `!is.na()` test comes first, so a missing final grade always gets "No".

```{r f5}
grades$Honors <- ifelse(!is.na(grades$FinalGrade) &
                        grades$FinalGrade >= 90 &
                        grades$Attendance >= 90, "Yes", "No")
table(grades$Honors)
```

**f.6 if ... else if inside a loop.** A plain `if` handles one value at a time, so the loop visits each row. The results go into a separate vector. That keeps the data frame at 12 columns.

```{r f6}
loop_remarks <- character(nrow(grades))

for (i in seq_len(nrow(grades))) {
  g <- grades$FinalGrade[i]

  if (is.na(g)) {
    loop_remarks[i] <- "Incomplete"
  } else if (g >= 90) {
    loop_remarks[i] <- "Excellent"
  } else if (g >= 85) {
    loop_remarks[i] <- "Very Good"
  } else if (g >= 80) {
    loop_remarks[i] <- "Good"
  } else if (g >= 75) {
    loop_remarks[i] <- "Fair"
  } else {
    loop_remarks[i] <- "Needs Improvement"
  }
}

identical(loop_remarks, grades$Remarks)
```

The result is `TRUE`, so the loop and the nested `ifelse()` give the same remarks.

**f.7 The Console test.** This chunk does not run during the knit, since it stops with an error. Type the line in the Console to see the message.

```{r f7, eval=FALSE}
if (grades$FinalGrade >= 75) print("Passed")
```

The column holds 15 values, so the condition returns 15 results, and one of them is `NA`. In R 4.2 and newer, `if` stops with the error "the condition has length > 1". Older versions print a warning and use only the first value. The loop avoids the problem. It passes one value at a time to `if`, and the `is.na()` test removes the `NA` case first.

**f.8 Summary.**

```{r f8}
table(grades$Result)
table(grades$AttendanceFlag)
table(grades$Honors)

# Passed: 10 students (4 Failed and 1 Incomplete)
# At Risk: 4 students (Mark Villanueva, Jenny Bautista, Carlo Mendoza, Daniel Flores)
# Honors candidates: 4 students (Maria Santos, Kristine Lopez, Liza Ramos, Sofia Domingo)
```

**f.9 Column check.**

```{r f9}
ncol(grades)
stopifnot(ncol(grades) == 12)
names(grades)
```

## Part D: Exporting Results to .csv

### Question #7

Export the full processed table. The argument `row.names = FALSE` stops R from adding a numbering column.

```{r export_all}
write.csv(grades, "students_grades_processed.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

Export the at-risk students. R writes the file only when at least one student is at risk.

```{r export_risk}
at_risk <- grades[grades$AttendanceFlag == "At Risk", ]

if (nrow(at_risk) > 0) {
  write.csv(at_risk, "at_risk_students.csv", row.names = FALSE)
  print(paste(nrow(at_risk), "at-risk students exported."))
} else {
  print("No at-risk students. No file written.")
}
```

Export the honors list.

```{r export_honors}
honors <- grades[grades$Honors == "Yes",
                 c("StudentID", "Name", "Section", "FinalGrade", "Attendance")]

if (nrow(honors) > 0) {
  write.csv(honors, "honors_list.csv", row.names = FALSE)
  print(paste(nrow(honors), "honors candidates exported."))
} else {
  print("No honors candidates this term.")
}
```

Verify the exports. Read each file back and compare it with the original.

```{r verify}
check_all <- read.csv("students_grades_processed.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
dim(check_all)
dim(grades)
colSums(is.na(check_all))
head(check_all)

check_risk <- read.csv("at_risk_students.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
dim(check_risk)

check_honors <- read.csv("honors_list.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
dim(check_honors)
```

The processed file has 15 rows and 12 columns, the same as `grades`. The at-risk file has 4 rows. The honors file has 4 rows and 5 columns.

### Question #8

The missing midterm appears as `NA` in the exported file. The `write.csv()` function writes `NA` for missing values by default. The `FinalGrade` of the same student also shows `NA`.

```{r q8}
write.csv(grades, "temp_with_rownames.csv")
temp_check <- read.csv("temp_with_rownames.csv")
names(temp_check)
dim(temp_check)
invisible(file.remove("temp_with_rownames.csv"))
```

Without `row.names = FALSE`, R adds a first column of row numbers with an empty header. R names that column `X` when the file is read back. The file then has 13 columns instead of 12, and the extra column holds no real data.

### Question #9

Build the Scholarship column with nested `ifelse()` calls. The missing grade comes first, then Full, then Partial.

```{r q9}
grades$Scholarship <- ifelse(is.na(grades$FinalGrade), "Pending",
                      ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 95 & grades$Attendance >= 90, "Full",
                      ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 85 & grades$Attendance >= 90, "Partial",
                             "None")))
```

Select the students with a Full or Partial scholarship.

```{r q9c}
qualified <- grades[grades$Scholarship %in% c("Full", "Partial"),
                    c("StudentID", "Name", "FinalGrade", "Attendance", "Scholarship")]
qualified
```

Export them with a guard.

```{r q9d}
if (nrow(qualified) > 0) {
  write.csv(qualified, "scholarship_candidates.csv", row.names = FALSE)
  print(paste(nrow(qualified), "scholarship candidates exported."))
} else {
  print("No students qualify for a scholarship.")
}
```

Count each category.

```{r q9e}
table(grades$Scholarship)
```

Sofia Domingo earns the one Full scholarship. Maria Santos, Angela Reyes, Kristine Lopez, and Liza Ramos earn Partial scholarships. Bea Navarro stays Pending. The other nine students get None.

### Question #10

```{r q10}
# 1. Any comparison with NA returns NA, and if() cannot run on NA.
#    Checking is.na() first handles the missing grade before the comparison.
# 2. The test FinalGrade < 75 returns NA for the missing grade, and ifelse()
#    passes that NA straight through. The student would show NA instead of "Incomplete".
# 3. Use ifelse() to fill a whole column or vector at once.
#    Use if ... else for one value, or to choose which block of code runs.
# 4. Reading the file back proves the export worked. It shows the right row count,
#    the right columns, and no stray row-number column.
```
